analysis.one_liner: Requires drugs developed with federal research funding to be priced no higher than in comparable wealthy countries.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in August 2026 with 14 Democratic cosponsors and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, which has taken no action on it since.
analysis.plain_summary: When a company develops a drug, vaccine, medical device, or gene therapy using federal research money, the bill requires that company to sign a 'reasonable pricing' agreement with the Department of Health and Human Services. The price cannot be higher than the median price charged in Canada and six other large, high-income countries. Companies must also publicly report their clinical trial costs, federal subsidies, and revenues, and the government can waive the price rule only after a public process.
analysis.who_benefits: Americans who need prescription drugs, vaccines, medical devices, and gene therapies developed with taxpayer-funded research. Today, a drug discovered with National Institutes of Health funding can be sold in the U.S. at a far higher price than the same drug sells for in Canada or Europe; the bill would bar that for the products it covers. It would also give the public a window into what these products actually cost to develop and how much revenue they earn.

how_it_helps.text: Requires every federal agency funding biomedical research to attach a reasonable pricing condition to its grants, contracts, and patent licenses, so products built with public money cannot be priced without limit [S2].
Caps the price at the median charged in Canada and six other large, high-income OECD countries, so U.S. residents pay no more than patients in peer nations [S2].
Requires manufacturers to report clinical trial costs, federal subsidies, and annual revenues, and requires HHS to make those reports public [S2].

Lets the Secretary consider mechanisms like shortening monopoly periods or lowering prices when revenues exceed targets, prices exceed a cost-per-health-benefit standard, or prices block patient access [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Drug, vaccine, device, and gene-therapy makers whose products benefited from federal research funding would earn less on U.S. sales than they currently do. An honest supporter would also acknowledge that somewhat lower returns on federally funded products could marginally reduce the incentive to invest in biomedical research, a tradeoff the bill itself asks the Secretary to weigh when writing rules.

drawbacks.text: The bill applies only to products developed with federal research funding, so many top-selling drugs discovered and developed entirely with private money would be untouched, limiting how much prices actually fall [S2].

The bill itself acknowledges the challenge of administering pricing agreements when third parties control the relevant intellectual property, and it requires HHS to balance price limits against 'robust incentives to invest in biomedical research and development' [S2].
The Secretary can waive the pricing obligation entirely upon finding it is in the public interest, which a future administration could use broadly to hollow out the requirement [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the subset of medicines built on taxpayer-funded research, the bill directly addresses a concrete problem: Americans paying more than patients in peer countries for products their own taxes helped create. The main cost is potentially somewhat weaker returns on publicly funded drug development, and the bill's coverage is narrower than its headline suggests since purely privately developed drugs are exempt. The waiver process is transparent but leaves real discretion to whichever administration is in power.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced in August 2026 and sent to the Energy and Commerce Committee, which has not scheduled any action on it; Congress is still in session, so its fate is undecided.

narrative.text: Rep. Val Hoyle introduced the bill on August 13, 2026, joined by seven original cosponsors, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce [S1].
The bill has 14 cosponsors, all Democrats [S3].
No further action has been taken since the referral to committee [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has won or lost; the status quo holds. Drug companies continue to charge U.S. patients prices above what the same taxpayer-funded products sell for in Canada and other peer countries, and the bill has not moved toward a vote.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Status quo: drug makers keep current prices

for.name: Rep. Val Hoyle
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill requiring reasonable pricing agreements for federally funded biomedical products.

for.name: Original cosponsors (Reps. Doggett, Stansbury, Takano, Norton, Tlaib, Jayapal, Casar)
14 House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Signed on in support of the bill.

against.name: House Committee on Energy and Commerce (Chair Brett Guthrie)
against.what_they_did: Has not scheduled the bill for a markup or any committee action since its referral in August 2026.

against.name: Pharmaceutical industry
against.role: Industry affected by international reference pricing
against.what_they_did: Pharmaceutical manufacturers have consistently opposed international reference-pricing policies in Congress and in federal negotiations, arguing they reduce revenue available for research and development.

sides.party_line_note: All 14 cosponsors are Democrats, and the bill sits in a committee chaired by a Republican with a Republican House majority, so no Republican support has appeared in the record [S3, S4].

industries.note: Companies that commercialize federally funded drugs, vaccines, and gene therapies would be barred from charging U.S. patients more than the median price in Canada and six peer countries, cutting the highest prices in their largest market. The same products would remain under patent, so the industry keeps its monopoly but on lower U.S. prices.
Devices and diagnostic tests developed with federal funding would fall under the same reasonable-pricing and reporting requirements as drugs, including public disclosure of trial costs and revenues.

industries.industry: Universities and technology-transfer offices licensing federally funded patents
industries.note: The bill attaches pricing conditions to licenses of federally funded patents and test data, so universities that license discoveries would see pricing obligations pass through to their licensees. Many of these institutions already operate under Bayh-Dole march-in rules requiring reasonable terms, and the bill explicitly leaves those existing requirements in place.

analysis.trajectory: The bill sits in the Energy and Commerce Committee with only Democratic cosponsors and no committee action scheduled. The large majority of bills referred to committee never reach the floor, and with no Republican support in the record, the realistic path is that the bill remains in committee and expires at the end of the 119th Congress unless sponsors build bipartisan support or attach it to a larger health package.
